chapters.title: The Surprising Power of Atomic Habits
chapters.sourcePressure: Tiny improvements compound, systems govern trajectory, and results often lag behind habit structure.
chapters.coreMove: Treat invisible progress as banked evidence and keep improving the system while results lag.
chapters.commonMisread: Thinking tiny habits are motivational slogans or that small effort deserves immediate visible payoff.

chapters.title: How Your Habits Shape Your Identity (and Vice Versa)
chapters.sourcePressure: Habits shape identity by turning repeated action into evidence for a self-concept, and identity-based change lasts longer than outcome-only chasing.
chapters.coreMove: Convert each repetition into a vote for the identity you want to make believable.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating identity as an affirmation instead of evidence earned by repeated behavior.

chapters.title: How to Build Better Habits in 4 Simple Steps
chapters.sourcePressure: Habits run through a practical loop of cue, craving, response, and reward, and the Four Laws are direct interventions on that loop.
chapters.coreMove: Diagnose a habit by locating the weak link in cue, craving, response, or reward.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing the habit loop to a memorized diagram rather than a troubleshooting tool.

chapters.title: The Man Who Didn't Look Right
chapters.sourcePressure: Awareness must come before change because automatic behavior often becomes too familiar to notice clearly.
chapters.coreMove: Catch the automatic routine at the cue level before trying to repair it.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming awareness alone fixes behavior or drifting into vague mindfulness.

chapters.title: The Best Way to Start a New Habit
chapters.sourcePressure: New habits start better when the cue is highly specific and attached to a stable routine or context.
chapters.coreMove: Attach the next habit to a precise existing cue so starting has a visible address.
chapters.commonMisread: Writing a broad intention instead of choosing an exact cue and location.

chapters.title: Motivation Is Overrated; Environment Often Matters More
chapters.sourcePressure: Behavior often follows what the environment makes visible, nearby, and easy to notice before motivation has to intervene.
chapters.coreMove: Place the desired cue where attention naturally lands before motivation is needed.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning environment design into decluttering advice or claiming motivation never matters.
mustNotDriftInto: friction engineering as the main idea

chapters.title: The Secret to Self-Control
chapters.sourcePressure: What looks like self-control often reflects encountering tempting cues less often rather than winning constant direct fights against them.
chapters.coreMove: Reduce exposure to tempting cues so discipline happens upstream of the urge.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating self-control as heroic resistance instead of fewer cue collisions.

chapters.title: How to Make a Habit Irresistible
chapters.sourcePressure: Cues become powerful not only when they are visible, but when they are linked to craving, anticipation, and attractive association.
chapters.coreMove: Pair a needed action with anticipation so the cue begins to pull instead of merely remind.
chapters.commonMisread: Confusing attraction with visible reminders or generic enthusiasm.

chapters.title: The Role of Family and Friends in Shaping Your Habits
chapters.sourcePressure: Habits become more attractive when they align with belonging, social norms, and the people around us.
chapters.coreMove: Choose or shape a group where the desired behavior protects belonging.
chapters.commonMisread: Claiming people blindly copy groups, instead of showing belonging changing what feels desirable.

chapters.title: How to Find and Fix the Causes of Your Bad Habits
chapters.sourcePressure: Bad habits often persist because they appear to solve a problem or relieve a feeling, and better change starts by naming that underlying cause accurately.
chapters.coreMove: Name the real relief a bad habit is buying before choosing a better response.
chapters.commonMisread: Calling the bad habit irrational before identifying the problem it seems to solve.

chapters.title: Walk Slowly, but Never Backward
chapters.sourcePressure: Progress comes from repeated action and accumulated reps, not from waiting for a flawless beginning.
chapters.coreMove: Move from planning into repeated reps before judging the habit by quality.
chapters.commonMisread: Equating motion with progress or using preparation to avoid the first imperfect rep.

chapters.title: The Law of Least Effort
chapters.sourcePressure: Behavior often follows the path of least resistance, so good habit design reduces friction for the desired action and increases friction for the unwanted one.
chapters.coreMove: Redraw the path so the desired action is the lower-friction default.
chapters.commonMisread: Using ease as laziness rather than as a deliberately designed path of least resistance.

chapters.title: How to Stop Procrastinating by Using the Two-Minute Rule
chapters.sourcePressure: Procrastination weakens when the first move is reduced to a tiny, easy entry action, often framed as a two-minute version of the habit.
chapters.coreMove: Shrink the doorway to the habit until starting is too small to refuse.
chapters.commonMisread: Pretending the two-minute version is the whole ambition rather than the entry ritual.
mustUseTerms: master the habit of showing up

chapters.title: How to Make Good Habits Inevitable and Bad Habits Impossible
chapters.sourcePressure: Good habits become far more likely when the environment keeps them available and ready, while bad habits weaken when stronger barriers make them hard to perform.
chapters.coreMove: Preload the environment so the good action is ready and the bad action is blocked.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating commitment devices as perfect control instead of stronger default design.

chapters.title: The Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change
chapters.sourcePressure: Behavior that feels satisfying now is more likely to be repeated, so good habits need some immediate reinforcement while bad habits often win because they reward immediately.
chapters.coreMove: Give the good habit an immediate satisfying signal while its larger payoff is still delayed.
chapters.commonMisread: Confusing lasting reward with immediate satisfaction, or making rewards so large they become the habit.

chapters.title: How to Stick with Good Habits Every Day
chapters.sourcePressure: Visible evidence and habit tracking can make repetition satisfying across days, but the practical recovery rule is to avoid missing twice in a row.
chapters.coreMove: Use visible tracking to return quickly after a miss instead of worshiping the streak.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning tracking into perfectionism, shame, or streak worship.

chapters.title: How an Accountability Partner Can Change Everything
chapters.sourcePressure: Accountability helps habits stick because another person or agreement makes the consequence of failing more immediate and harder to ignore.
chapters.coreMove: Make follow-through visible to another person so consequences arrive in the present.
chapters.commonMisread: Using accountability as embarrassment instead of present consequence and support.

chapters.title: The Truth About Talent (When Genes Matter and When They Don't)
chapters.sourcePressure: People differ in natural tendencies and strengths, so habits compound best when the chosen behavior or field fits those tendencies rather than fighting them blindly.
chapters.coreMove: Select habits and arenas where natural tendencies make effort compound faster.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating genes as destiny or using fit as an excuse to avoid hard work.

chapters.title: The Goldilocks Rule: How to Stay Motivated in Life and Work
chapters.sourcePressure: Motivation stays strongest when the task is just hard enough to demand attention without tipping into discouragement or boredom.
chapters.coreMove: Keep the challenge at the edge of ability so attention stays alive.
chapters.commonMisread: Mistaking calibrated challenge for constant novelty, grind, or maximum difficulty.

chapters.title: The Downside of Creating Good Habits
chapters.sourcePressure: Good habits create efficiency, but automatic repetition can hide mistakes, drift, and stagnation unless the person pauses to review and refine the routine deliberately.
chapters.coreMove: Interrupt automatic competence with review so repetition keeps improving rather than concealing drift.
chapters.commonMisread: Ending with a generic recap instead of showing how automaticity can hide mistakes.
